question: how seismically active is this location, as a long-run rate of M+ events per year
source: USGS ComCat (earthquake.usgs.gov), public domain, no API key
limitations: This is a long-run rate, not a forecast. It does not predict that an earthquake will happen, when, or how large; it says how active the region has been. A short window probability derived from it is correspondingly small, and should not be read as a prediction.

Only M5.0+ is counted, on the grounds that the catalogue is near-complete globally at that level. A lower floor would mostly measure local network instrumentation, and would make quiet regions look active purely because they are well monitored.
Aftershocks are not declustered. A single mainshock sequence can dominate a cell's count, so a cell's rate is a floor on its activity rather than a clean independent-event rate.

Cells holding fewer than 2 events are omitted, so 4043 of 47922 catalogue events are not represented. A location in an omitted cell reads as zero rate, which means 'not enough events to say', not 'no earthquakes'.
The rate is spatially binned, not area-weighted, so a cell's count is attributed to its centre. Locations near a cell edge inherit the cell's rate regardless of which side of the edge they fall on.

The magnitude floor is applied to the catalogue, not to the peak magnitude, so this says nothing about the severity of any event that does occur -- that is the attenuation model's job, not this prior's.

The window spans about 27 years. Seismicity is not stationary over that span: the rate for any given decade may differ from the mean, and cluster bursts make short recent windows unrepresentative either way.
